title: Dissipative phase transitions in quantum reservoir computing
abstract: Enhanced performance of quantum reservoir computing has been associated with dynamical phase transitions, but whether this connection extends to dissipative systems and which relaxation mechanisms underlie it remain insufficiently understood. We systematically compare driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions and find enhanced memory and nonlinear processing near both phase boundaries. Although the closure of the Liouvillian gap marks the transitions in the thermodynamic limit, computational performance does not generally follow gap suppression. An exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition quantitatively attributes the trained memory to intrinsic relaxation channels. It shows that the gap mode contributes only weakly, while finite-rate modes and their cross-contributions dominate the enhanced capacity. These results go beyond phenomenological correlations by directly linking memory capacity to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum. Moreover, these findings provide a physical basis for designing dissipative quantum reservoirs and testing memory-enhancement mechanisms in experimentally accessible Kerr platforms.
summary: This work investigates how quantum reservoir computing performs near dissipative phase transitions in Kerr reservoirs. The authors find that while performance peaks near these transitions, the underlying mechanism is not simply the closing of the spectral gap. Instead, the enhanced memory capacity is quantitatively attributed to the reorganization of faster, finite-rate relaxation modes within the system's Liouvillian spectrum.
main_problem: To determine if enhanced performance in Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) near dissipative phase transitions is linked to the Liouvillian gap closure, and to identify the specific relaxation mechanisms responsible for this enhancement.
main_result: The enhanced memory capacity is dominated not by the slowest relaxation mode (the gap mode), but by the reorganization and contributions of finite-rate relaxation channels.
method: The authors use mode-resolved decomposition of the trained Information Processing Capacity (IPC) by analyzing the Liouvillian spectrum and attributing computational relevance to specific relaxation channels.
model_or_system: The study analyzes driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs, modeled by a master equation incorporating linear and quadratic driving terms, exhibiting both first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions.
key_observables: Information Processing Capacity (IPC), Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) for NARMA, and the Liouvillian relaxation spectrum ($\lambda_\mu$).
important_parameters: Tuning parameters ($\zeta$), the Liouvillian gap ($\Lambda$), and the decay rates ($\Gamma_\mu$) of the relaxation modes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the system dynamics can be accurately described by the Liouvillian formalism and that the trained memory can be decomposed into contributions from individual relaxation modes.
figures_summary: Figures show performance optima near transitions, spectral reorganization patterns (e.g., localized compression vs. gap softening), and modal attribution confirming finite-rate modes dominate capacity.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the QRC model, analyzes the Liouvillian spectrum across different transitions, develops a mode-resolved attribution technique, and concludes by showing that task-relevant capacity tracks finite-rate dynamics rather than gap closure.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative link between the spectral properties of open quantum systems (Liouvillian spectrum) and information processing capabilities, offering a new diagnostic tool for designing dissipative quantum devices.
